clue.text: Leave supporter for one expected to rise to great heights

definitions.text: one expected to rise to great heights

parts.note: to leave is to go
a sling supports an injured arm

explanation.surface: A Brexit 'Leave' backer is tipped as a rising political star.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leave supporter' reads as a Brexiteer, but it splits into a verb and a bandage.
explanation.definitionFit: A young goose is expected to grow into a bird that flies at great altitude.

clue.text: Mute panic when swimming is related to air supply

indicators.note: letters that are swimming move about freely, so the words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A diver's silent panic underwater turns out to be connected to the air supply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when swimming' signals rearranging MUTE PANIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Pneumatic devices and tyres work by compressed air, so the word describes anything related to air.

clue.text: Massage will reportedly cause irritation

indicators.note: signals that the words are heard spoken rather than spelt out

parts.note: to massage is to knead; 'll is the short form of will

explanation.surface: A rubdown, rumour has it, will only cause irritation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reportedly' signals that KNEAD'LL is heard, not spelt.
explanation.definitionFit: To needle someone is to provoke or annoy them with persistent jibes.

clue.text: Bizarre content-free media column shared by everybody

indicators.note: something bizarre is odd and twisted, so the letters are rearranged
with its contents removed only the word's outside letters stay

explanation.surface: A weird, empty newspaper column that every reader shares.
explanation.walkthrough: 'content-free' empties MEDIA to MA; 'Bizarre' rearranges MA with COLUMN.
explanation.definitionFit: Communal property or space is held in common, belonging to the whole group.

clue.text: Lady disheartened after exchanging letters in a fitting manner

indicators.note: the first piece is placed after the second, so it comes first in the answer here

parts.note: people corresponding write letters to each other

indicators.note: losing its heart, the word keeps only its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A lady loses heart after swapping letters with a pen-friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exchanging letters' looks like a lovers' quarrel but means writing to each other; 'disheartened' leaves only the outside letters of Lady, and 'after' places them at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Correspondingly means in a matching or analogous way, suiting the situation.

clue.text: Staff getting on and coping with difficulties

parts.note: to staff a post is to man it
someone getting on is ageing

explanation.surface: Older employees struggling to cope with problems.
explanation.definitionFit: Managing means getting by or handling things despite hardship.

clue.text: Preventative measure quashed by jury rejecting case associated with settlement

indicators.note: in a down clue, a piece quashed by another sits beneath it
throwing away its case removes the word's outer letters

parts.note: a ban prevents something

explanation.surface: A ban is overturned by a jury that throws out the case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejecting case' strips JURY to UR; 'quashed by' puts BAN below it in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Urban describes a town or city, a large human settlement.

clue.text: Praise responsible individual's time in A&E

indicators.note: the time letter is shifted so it sits inside the A and E pair

parts.note: an adult is a grown person held responsible
taken as its two letters

explanation.surface: Praise the grown-up who spent hours waiting in a hospital emergency department.
explanation.walkthrough: The T at the end of ADULT is moved, 'in', between A and E. A&E is a British hospital's emergency department.
explanation.definitionFit: To adulate is to flatter or admire someone excessively.

clue.text: Measure associated with the pound follows British economic recovery

indicators.note: the measure comes after the abbreviation

parts.note: the ounce is a weight unit, sixteen to the pound

explanation.surface: A rise in the pound follows a British economic recovery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the pound' looks like sterling, but it is the weight.
explanation.definitionFit: A bounce is a quick rebound, as when an economy picks up after a fall.

clue.text: This car could convey 6

parts.note: split 5,3, the entry reads as an instruction: its last three letters signal an anagram of its first five, which spells the entry at 6 Down

explanation.surface: This vehicle could carry a city dweller.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer RUNAB OUT: 'out' is an anagram indicator, and RUNAB rearranged is URBAN (6 Down). 'This' just points to the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A runabout is a small light car for short local trips.

clue.text: Struggle ineffectually, being near the bottom in the main

definitions.text: being near the bottom in the main
definitions.meaning: a flatfish living on the seabed; 'the main' is the sea

explanation.surface: Floundering near the foot of the main league table.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to struggle clumsily; the noun is a bottom-dwelling flatfish in the ocean.

clue.text: He may buy rounds and drain bottle after golf

indicators.note: the second piece comes after the first

parts.note: Golf is the NATO alphabet word for G
to unman is to drain someone's courage, 'bottle' being British slang for nerve

explanation.surface: A golfer who buys rounds of drinks and empties a bottle at the nineteenth hole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rounds' are of ammunition, not drinks; 'bottle' is British slang for courage.
explanation.definitionFit: A gunman purchases rounds, that is bullets, for his firearm.

clue.text: Peacekeepers clearing tense area of Tours goes wrong

parts.note: UN peacekeepers belong to the United Nations

indicators.note: clearing a letter from the word takes it out

parts.note: tours means travels
T is the grammar abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: UN peacekeepers clearing a tense area near the French city of Tours, and it goes wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tours' looks like the French city; it is the verb TRAVELS, and 'clearing' takes T out.
explanation.definitionFit: A plan that unravels comes apart and fails.

clue.text: Beat criminal up in Slough

indicators.note: something criminal is crooked, so the letters are bent into a new order

parts.note: to slough a skin is to shed it

explanation.surface: A villain was beaten up in the town of Slough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'criminal' rearranges UP IN; Slough looks like the English town west of London but is the verb meaning shed.
explanation.definitionFit: Beat here is past tense: punished as in physically chastised.

clue.text: What addict maybe did to obtain free drugs once?

definitions.text: What addict maybe did to obtain

indicators.note: set free, the letters are released into a new order

explanation.surface: Asks what a user did to get free narcotics in the old days.
explanation.walkthrough: 'free' looks like 'at no cost' but signals rearranging DRUGS ONCE.
explanation.definitionFit: To scrounge is to beg or cadge something without paying, as an addict might.

clue.text: Substance turning up in drug ingested by couriers

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up reads the result from bottom to top
something ingested goes inside the swallower

parts.note: drug mules carry drugs for smugglers
E is shorthand for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A substance turns up in drugs swallowed by smugglers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ingested by' puts IN and E into MULES (MUINELES); 'turning up' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: Selenium is a chemical element, a basic substance.

clue.text: Start school dropping every second set of courses

indicators.note: each word loses its second letter

parts.note: to launch is to start
Eton is the famous English public school

explanation.surface: Starting school by dropping half the courses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dropping every second' takes A from LAUNCH and T from ETON.
explanation.definitionFit: A luncheon is a formal midday meal served in several courses.

clue.text: Rid one's mind of tragic figure stopping sister cycling

indicators.note: a piece stopping another is lodged inside it
cycling the letters moves the first one to the end

parts.note: a nun is a religious sister
King Lear is Shakespeare's tragic hero

explanation.surface: Forgetting about a tragic figure who stops his sister cycling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cycling' moves the first letter of the sister to the end, giving UNN, and 'stopping' lodges Shakespeare's king inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To unlearn something is to deliberately forget it or discard it.

clue.text: Back objective to replace leader in Hackney?

indicators.note: the new word takes the place of the first letter

parts.note: a hackney is a breed of horse
an end is an objective

explanation.surface: Supporting a goal of replacing the leader of Hackney council.
explanation.walkthrough: Hackney looks like the London borough, but it is a breed of horse; END replaces its H.
explanation.definitionFit: To endorse is to support or back a proposal or candidate.

clue.text: Ignore importance of aristocratic underworld figure?

parts.note: Dis is the Roman god of the underworld
a count is an aristocrat

explanation.surface: Dismissing how important a posh gangland boss is.
explanation.walkthrough: Split 3,5 the answer is a count of the underworld, so 'underworld figure' looks like a gangster but is the god.
explanation.definitionFit: To discount something is to disregard it or treat it as unimportant.

clue.text: Wicked king's not part of reason for incoherent state

indicators.note: the letter is taken out of the longer word

parts.note: a skinful is enough drink to make one drunk
K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A wicked king takes no part in explaining why the nation is in chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: SKINFUL is British slang for enough alcohol to get drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Sinful means morally wrong or wicked.

clue.text: Dive practice on vacation includes breathing apparatus

indicators.note: the outer piece holds the other inside it
vacated, the word loses its inside letters, leaving its ends

parts.note: a lung is the organ of breathing

explanation.surface: Diving practice on holiday involves scuba gear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on vacation' empties practice to its first and last letters, and 'includes' wraps them round the organ of breathing.
explanation.definitionFit: A plunge is a sudden headlong dive into water.

clue.text: Present Only Connect, wanting both sides to get involved

indicators.note: letters that get involved become tangled, so they are rearranged
lacking both ends, the word loses its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A gift for the TV quiz Only Connect, minus the edges, to get people involved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wanting both sides' trims CONNECT to ONNEC; 'to get involved' rearranges it. Only Connect is a BBC quiz show.
explanation.definitionFit: The nonce is the present occasion, as in the phrase 'for the nonce'.

clue.text: New College hampered by twelve working with no representation

indicators.note: the pieces are hemmed in by the outer word

parts.note: noon is twelve o'clock
uni is short for university, a college

explanation.surface: A new Oxford college held back by a dozen staff with no representation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New College' looks like the Oxford college; 'working' belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Non-union workers do not belong to a trade union representing them.

clue.text: Wild dog almost biting relative is rather scary

indicators.note: the outer piece bites, holding the other in its jaws
almost the whole word, losing its last letter

parts.note: the dingo is the Australian wild dog
an aunt is a relative

explanation.surface: A feral dog nearly biting a family member is fairly frightening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' drops the last letter of the Australian wild dog to give DING, and 'biting' closes it round the relative.
explanation.definitionFit: Daunting means intimidating, likely to make someone lose courage.

clue.text: Misfortune, as expected, brings discomfort with it

indicators.note: the opening words bring the answer along inside them, concealed in their letters

explanation.surface: Bad luck, predictably, causes distress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brings ... with it' tells you the answer runs through MisfortUNE AS Expected.
explanation.definitionFit: Unease is a feeling of anxiety or disquiet.

clue.text: Funny scene employs 'characters', regularly appearing inappropriate

indicators.note: only letters at regular intervals appear, here every second one

explanation.surface: A comic scene uses actors who keep turning up unsuitably.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly appearing' takes the even letters of FUNNY SCENE EMPLOYS.
explanation.definitionFit: Unseemly behaviour is improper or not in good taste.
